title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
hookLine: an African official reads Isaiah in his chariot and asks, what hinders me?
last: LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.

lines: A CHARIOT ON THE DESERT ROAD.
cards: Ever been stuck on a page? A tax form, a poem for school, a medicine label: you read it three times and the words just sit there.
On a desert road south from Jerusalem toward Gaza, a chariot rolls along, carrying an important man: the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of all her wealth.
He's been to Jerusalem to worship, a long trip from Africa, and heading home he's reading a scroll of the prophet Isaiah out loud. And he's stuck.
Meanwhile an angel has told Philip, one of the seven food organizers, to go and stand on that road. Just that.

teach.b: The Spirit tells Philip to go up to the chariot, so he runs alongside and hears him reading. He asks, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?"

teach.h: HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?
teach.b: The answer is plain: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up. The passage is Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent, humiliated.
Who is the prophet talking about, the man asks, himself or someone else? And Philip, starting from that page, tells him about Jesus.
In the background, the official is called a eunuch, and Deuteronomy says a eunuch may not enter the assembly of the Lord.
But a few chapters on in the very scroll he's holding, God promises eunuchs who keep his covenant a place, and a name that will never be cut off. Whether he'd read that far, the text doesn't say.

At some water by the road he asks the question of the day: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" In the King James text, Philip's only condition is that he believe with all his heart.
They go down into the water, and he's baptized.

teach.h: HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.
teach.b: Philip is suddenly gone, and the official goes on his way rejoicing. Scholars think the Ethiopia of Acts was the kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in what's now Sudan.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church treasures the story all the same. Some readers hear a quiet echo of Pentecost: the good news heading toward the ends of the earth, one reader at a time.

how: Christians often read the story of Philip and the Ethiopian as a picture of the good news reaching Africa and of baptism welcoming someone once kept at the edge. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds the story especially dear.

games.q: you're the official. a stranger has explained your page of Isaiah, and now there's water by the road. what do you say?
o: thank you. I'll think about it at home.
see, here is water; what hinders me?
games.why: he asks, what doth hinder me to be baptized? they go down into the water, and he goes on his way rejoicing.

practice: Think of someone who's stuck on something you understand: a kid with homework, a parent with a phone, a friend with a form.
Philip runs to catch up, asks a question first, and starts from the exact page they're on, not where he'd like to start; picture doing that, gently, without a sigh. If you pray, pray for that person.

wordCard.voice: Eunuch. The title Acts gives the Ethiopian official, a man the law once excluded, whom Philip baptizes anyway, right by the road.

orig.note: Greek: hinders, prevents. The official's question is ti kolyei me: what hinders me?

carryVoice: Your line: what hinders you? Tomorrow, the young man who held the coats meets a light on the road. See you there.
